title: The Simulator as a System Component
summary: Work through The Simulator as a System Component.

sections: The Simulator as a System Component
Massively parallel simulation and on-policy learning

blocks.md: This lesson follows **The Simulator as a System Component** in *Policy Training* (Vol IV).

blocks.source: Vol IV, Policy Training, § The Simulator as a System Component
blocks.md: A reinforcement learning policy trained on door latching learned an aggressive, unbraked plunge because its simulated strike plate yielded far more than the physical mechanism. Stripping away the simulator during physical deployment does nothing to unlearn that behavior. The physics simulator is not an external sandbox; it is an active component of the training pipeline whose equations, contact approximations, and timing assumptions dictate the exact experience supplied to the optimizer. Accepting simulated task success as evidence of hardware readiness requires measurable, verifiable error bounds on every one of those assumptions.

questions.q: The section **The Simulator as a System Component** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A decoder chosen for multimodality must fit the proposal deadline, since latency is encoding plus every dependent decoder evaluation, so the head and evaluation count that training picks decide schedulability.
A simulator's contact model decides what the optimizer learns, and a soft penalty spring lets a policy pass through contacts the real plate would resist.

A policy's weights keep what its experience rewarded but not which experience it was, so each regime (demonstrations, logged rewards, simulation, trial on the machine, a pretrained base) leaves a characteristic dependency no training score shows.
State value, action value, advantage, and the Bellman relation express value as negated cost-to-go, with LQR as the closed-form linear-quadratic case.
